The polyglot backend

polyglot-backend.Rmd

You write R. Underneath, polyviz talks to whatever engine fits the job: SQLite for data that lives in a database, haven for SAS files and their variable labels, an optional Python module for numeric profiling, and D3.js for every chart. This vignette shows each seam — and makes the point that none of them require you to leave R, or even to notice which engine did the work.

One reader for every file

pv_read() dispatches on the file extension: CSV and RDS via base R, .sas7bdat/.xpt via haven, .sqlite/.db via DBI. The package bundles a small SQLite database to demonstrate:

db <- system.file("extdata", "demo.sqlite", package = "polyviz")
sales <- pv_read(db, table = "sales")
head(sales, 3)
#>    date   month region product units  revenue
#> 1 19723 2024-01   East   Aster   311 38456.03
#> 2 19723 2024-01   East  Betula   463 40470.83
#> 3 19723 2024-01   East  Cedrus   111 22996.73

SQL, when the data lives in a database

For anything beyond “give me the table”, open a real connection and push work to the database. Aggregating in SQL and charting the small result in R is the natural division of labour:

con <- pv_db_connect(db)
pv_db_tables(con)
#> [1] "product_dim" "sales"

by_region <- pv_query(con, "
  SELECT region, SUM(revenue) AS revenue
  FROM sales
  GROUP BY region
  ORDER BY revenue DESC
")
by_region
#>   region revenue
#> 1  North 5510015
#> 2   East 4681281
#> 3   West 4280677
#> 4  South 3846500

Parameters are bound with ? placeholders — values never get pasted into the SQL string:

pv_query(con,
  "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM sales WHERE region = ? AND units > ?",
  params = list("North", 300))
#>    n
#> 1 76

The result of a query is an ordinary data frame, so it flows straight into a chart:

pv_bar(by_region, x = "region", y = "revenue",
       title = "Aggregated by SQLite, drawn by D3",
       subtitle = "Revenue by region, summed in the database")

Schema and seed scripts can stay as plain .sql files and run with pv_run_sql_file(). Scratch databases work the same way — pv_db_connect() with no path opens an in-memory one, and pv_db_write() puts any data frame into it.

pv_db_disconnect(con)

SAS, without SAS

haven reads and writes SAS files directly, so polyviz can round-trip them — including variable labels, the SAS metadata that usually gets lost in translation. Attach labels, write an .xpt transport file, read it back:

labelled <- pv_set_labels(mtcars[1:4], c(
  mpg = "Miles per US gallon",
  cyl = "Number of cylinders",
  disp = "Displacement (cu in)",
  hp = "Gross horsepower"
))

xpt <- tempfile(fileext = ".xpt")
pv_write_sas(labelled, xpt)

back <- pv_read_sas(xpt)
pv_labels(back)
#>                    mpg                    cyl                   disp 
#>  "Miles per US gallon"  "Number of cylinders" "Displacement (cu in)" 
#>                     hp 
#>     "Gross horsepower"

The labels survive the trip, and downstream tools use them: pv_summary() shows a label column whenever one is present.

pv_summary(back)
#> <pv_summary> 32 rows x 4 cols | 100.0% complete cases
#> 
#>  variable label                class   n_missing pct_missing n_distinct
#>  mpg      Miles per US gallon  numeric 0         0           25        
#>  cyl      Number of cylinders  numeric 0         0            3        
#>  disp     Displacement (cu in) numeric 0         0           27        
#>  hp       Gross horsepower     numeric 0         0           22        
#>  sketch                    
#>  10.4 to 33.9 (median 19.2)
#>  4 to 8 (median 6)         
#>  71.1 to 472 (median 196)  
#>  52 to 335 (median 123)

Python, when it happens to be there

Numeric profiling (pv_profile(), pv_outliers()) can run on a small Python module bundled with the package, via reticulate. The rule: Python is never required. Every Python-backed function has a pure-R implementation that returns identical results, and engine = "auto" (the default) quietly picks whichever is available.

pv_py_available()
#> [1] TRUE

prof <- pv_profile(mtcars[c("mpg", "hp", "wt")])
attr(prof, "engine")
#> [1] "python"
prof
#>   variable  n n_missing      mean         sd    min      q25  median    q75
#> 1      mpg 32         0  20.09062  6.0269481 10.400 15.42500  19.200  22.80
#> 2       hp 32         0 146.68750 68.5628685 52.000 96.50000 123.000 180.00
#> 3       wt 32         0   3.21725  0.9784574  1.513  2.58125   3.325   3.61
#>       max  skewness    kurtosis  jb_stat      jb_p
#> 1  33.900 0.6404399 -0.20053321 2.241155 0.3260914
#> 2 335.000 0.7614356  0.05223273 3.095820 0.2126920
#> 3   5.424 0.4437855  0.17247054 1.090038 0.5798308

On a machine with Python, that engine attribute reads "python"; on one without, "r" — and the numbers are the same either way, which the package’s test suite asserts. Forcing a specific engine is explicit: engine = "r" always works, engine = "python" errors (rather than silently downgrading) when Python is missing.

identical(prof$mean, pv_profile(mtcars[c("mpg", "hp", "wt")],
                                engine = "r")$mean)
#> [1] TRUE

JavaScript: what actually travels to D3

Every chart function builds a plain payload — data as row-wise records, options, and the colour theme — and hands it to the bundled D3 v7 renderers through htmlwidgets. No JavaScript is written at chart time, and you can inspect exactly what crosses the boundary:

w <- pv_bar(by_region, x = "region", y = "revenue")
names(w$x)
#>  [1] "data"        "xlab"        "ylab"        "stack"       "horizontal" 
#>  [6] "valueLabels" "title"       "subtitle"    "mode"        "duration"   
#> [11] "source"      "type"        "theme"       "alt"
str(w$x$data)
#> 'data.frame':    4 obs. of  2 variables:
#>  $ x: chr  "North" "East" "West" "South"
#>  $ y: num  5510015 4681281 4280677 3846500

type picks the renderer, theme carries the full light and dark token sets (the browser picks at render time, following the viewer’s system preference), and modifiers like pv_trend() just add fields to this list: the loess or lm fit runs in R, and only the fitted points travel to JavaScript. R stays the single source of statistical truth; D3 only draws.

Coming back: events and linked selections

The boundary runs both ways. Inside a Shiny app, every chart reports interactions as input values named <outputId>_<event>:

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  pvchartOutput("revenue"),
  verbatimTextOutput("detail")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$revenue <- renderPvchart(
    pv_bar(by_region, x = "region", y = "revenue")
  )
  # Clicking a bar arrives here as input$revenue_click.
  output$detail <- renderPrint(input$revenue_click)
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

And without any server at all, pv_link() joins charts through a crosstalk selection group — brushing points in one chart dims the non-matching marks in every linked widget, even in a static HTML page:

f25 <- subset(pv_fiscal, year == 2025)
sd <- crosstalk::SharedData$new(f25)

# Both charts are built from the same rows and linked to the same
# group: selecting municipalities in the scatter highlights them on
# the map, and vice versa.
htmltools::browsable(htmltools::tagList(
  pv_scatter(f25, x = "resource_index", y = "equalization_chf",
             label = "municipality") |> pv_link(sd),
  pv_choropleth(f25, id = "municipality_id",
                value = "resource_index") |> pv_link(sd)
))

Four engines, one interface — and the seams only show when you go looking for them.
